name: FireDucks
workload: TPC-H at Scale Factor 10 (~10GB), all 22 queries, both excluding I/O (RUN_IO_TYPE=skip) and including I/O (RUN_IO_TYPE=parquet), on AWS EC2 m7i.8xlarge (Intel Xeon Gold 6526Y, 32 cores, 512GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04, performance governor)
claimed_speedup: Average speedup over pandas across 22 TPC-H queries: FireDucks 141x (excl. I/O) / 55x (incl. I/O); for comparison on the same page, DuckDB 109x/61x and Polars 58x/50x
hardware: AWS EC2 m7i.8xlarge, Intel Xeon Gold 6526Y (32 cores), 512GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04, cpufreq-governor=performance
stars_or_usage: 927 stars on the GitHub issue-tracker repo; NEC-backed commercial project, widely cited in dataframe-benchmark discussions
tradeoffs: Drop-in pandas replacement via import hook; compiler-accelerated lazy execution graph. The engine itself is closed-source: this GitHub repo is issue-tracker only (no source files), the wheel is distributed via PyPI, and only Linux x86_64 is supported.
caveats: License is a PyPI trove classifier claim (BSD License / README says 3-Clause BSD) rather than a browsable OSI-licensed source repo, so usability is recorded as reference, not copyable. Benchmark is first-party (FireDucks' own docs site), though methodology (versions, hardware, scale factor) is unusually well documented for a first-party page. Repo has had no push since 2025-05-22.
found_via: HN Algolia query 'faster than polars' -> 'FireDucks: 125x faster than Pandas, 2.2x faster than polars' -> fireducks-dev.github.io/docs/benchmarks/

name: Minarrow
workload: Sum of 1,000 i64 integers averaged over 1,000 runs, comparing raw Vec<i64>, Minarrow's IntegerArray (direct and via enum dispatch), and arrow-rs's Int64Array (struct and dyn-dispatched), plus a separate Rust<->Python zero-copy roundtrip test on 1M rows x 2 columns via PyO3
claimed_speedup: IntegerArray direct access: 88ns vs Arrow-rs Int64Array (struct) 147ns and Arrow-rs Int64Array (dyn) 181ns -- roughly 1.7x-2.1x faster (derived from page data). Rust->Python handoff for 1M rows/2 cols: 165ns.
tradeoffs: Deliberately minimal Arrow implementation (no List/Struct nested types yet); nightly Rust toolchain required for allocator_api/portable_simd; requires CLA for contributions. Gains come from a leaner enum-dispatch array representation vs arrow-rs's more general struct/dyn-trait design, not from a different algorithm.
caveats: This is a micro-benchmark of a single primitive (scalar sum over a small array), not a full query-engine workload; results may not generalize to larger analytical queries. Benchmark code lives in examples rather than a dedicated bench harness with published raw data.
found_via: HN Algolia query 'faster than polars' -> 'Show HN: Minarrow – Fast Rust columnar engine with Apache Arrow compatibility'

name: csvql
workload: SQL aggregates/GROUP BY/JOIN/LIKE queries run directly against raw CSV files (no ingest), at multiple scales: 2M rows/56MB, 5M rows/173MB, and the canonical NYC Taxi 20M rows/8GB CSV benchmark, on Apple M2 Pro / M-series hardware (one section on a cloud Intel Xeon VM, called out as not comparable across sections)
claimed_speedup: 2M-row aggregates: 6.8x-11.3x faster than DuckDB (e.g. COUNT(*) 0.012s vs 0.136s); joins: 9x-89x faster; LIKE queries: ~19x-36x faster; NYC Taxi 20M-row/8GB CSV: ~3.1x-3.4x faster with ~6x less peak memory (engine versions: csvql 2.6.0, DuckDB 1.5.5)
hardware: Apple M2 Pro / Apple M-series (one section: cloud VM, Intel Xeon, 4 cores)
tradeoffs: Read-only (SELECT only, no INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), single-file CSV-in-place querying via mmap, no persistent storage engine; join output order is undefined for parallelism. Positioned as an MCP tool for LLM agents to query large CSVs cheaply rather than a general OLAP replacement.
caveats: First-party benchmark; Zig build/compiler flags are not stated (only hardware and software versions), so this is capped at tier C rather than A per methodology rules. One section explicitly warns results from a different machine are not comparable to the rest. Author's own writeup documents a prior regression (a ~20x loss on IN-subquery at one data size) found and fixed, which is a point in favor of the benchmark's honesty but also shows performance is workload-sensitive.
found_via: HN Algolia query 'faster than duckdb' -> 'Csvql – SQL queries on CSV files, 9x faster than DuckDB, written in Zig'

name: Parquet Sort (Earnix)
workload: Read, sort (bucket sort on l_shipdate), and write a 59-million-row TPC-H SF10 lineitem.parquet file, on AWS EC2 c7i.4xlarge (16 vCPUs, 32GB RAM, gp3 SSD)
claimed_speedup: Time to sort: DuckDB 1.3.2 = 20.54s; Parquet Sort on Corretto 24 = 18.34s; on GraalVM 24 (JIT) = 24.47s; on GraalVM Native Image = 16.30s -- about 1.26x faster than DuckDB in the native-image build (derived from page data)
hardware: AWS EC2 c7i.4xlarge, 16 vCPUs, 32GB RAM, Amazon Linux 2023 (kernel 6.1.147), gp3 SSD 16000 IOPS/1000MiB/s, XFS
tradeoffs: Only implements sort (not a general query engine); relies on the author's own ParquetForge library; column-wise in-memory reordering means peak memory scales with column size; GraalVM Native build required to beat DuckDB (the plain JIT build was slower than DuckDB in this test).
caveats: First-party, single-workload benchmark (sort only) with no explicit JVM/native-image build flags stated, so capped at tier C. Margin over DuckDB is modest (~1.26x) and only achieved in the GraalVM Native configuration; the default Corretto JIT build (18.34s) is close to DuckDB and GraalVM JIT (24.47s) is slower than DuckDB.
found_via: HN Algolia query 'faster than duckdb' -> 'Show HN: Read Sort and Write Parquet Faster Than DuckDB in Java'

name: Tessera
workload: Backward as-of join (merge_asof semantics) of 1,000,000 trades against 1,000,000 quotes across 500 symbols, on a single dev laptop with .NET 9
claimed_speedup: Tessera merge-sweep: 10.8ms mean (~92M rows/s, 11.4MB allocated) vs pandas.merge_asof: 152.8ms (~6.5M rows/s) -- about 14x faster; also ~7.7x faster than a per-symbol binary-search join implemented in C#
tradeoffs: Requires inputs pre-sorted by time; join key must be a dense int code (via provided Categoricals.Factorize helpers); no out-of-core / memory-mapped support yet; narrow scope (as-of join + OHLCV bars + a few vectorized column ops), not a general dataframe library.
caveats: Very small, early, single-author project (1 star, ~1 month old at last commit) with no CPU model stated for the benchmark machine, capping evidence at tier C. The comparison is a single specialized operation (merge_asof), not general dataframe performance.
found_via: gh search repos "faster than pandas" --sort stars --limit 30 -> bpmcginley/Tessera

name: tickdb (DerekNest)
workload: 2,000,000 synthetic trade rows: on-disk size per trade (custom delta-of-delta timestamp + delta/zigzag price encoding + RLE + zstd, vs Parquet+zstd), plus OHLCV/VWAP/top-10-by-volume query throughput vs DuckDB and Polars, 2 runs on the author's machine
claimed_speedup: Storage: 6.50 bytes/trade vs 8.13 bytes/trade for Parquet+zstd -- about 20% smaller (derived from page data). Query speed: tickdb is NOT faster -- DuckDB beats it by 1.5x-1.6x on OHLCV, ~190-240x on VWAP, and ~55-115x on top-10-by-volume, per the project's own honestly-reported numbers.
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (self-described systems-engineering portfolio project, not for production quant use)
tradeoffs: Explicitly a learning/portfolio project, not production-ready; the only genuine performance win documented is on-disk compactness, not query speed -- author's own doc states DuckDB's vectorized execution engine beats tickdb on every benchmarked query shape.
caveats: No license file (GitHub reports no license), so the code cannot legally be reused despite being public -- recorded as usability=reference. Baseline for the one real win (storage size) is Parquet+zstd, not one of Arrow/DuckDB/ClickHouse/pandas/polars directly, so baseline_in_list=false. Included specifically because the project's benchmark doc is unusually candid about where it loses, per the task's instruction to record shortcomings honestly; it does not qualify as "faster" on any query-speed axis, only on storage footprint.
found_via: gh search repos "10x faster" olap columnar --sort stars --limit 30 -> DerekNest/tickdb
